explanations.explanation: A wind, friend. That's all it takes. "And God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to subside." (Genesis 8:1) No big show, just a wind, and the water starts heading down.

A pillar of fire does show up in the Bible, but later, when God leads Israel through the wilderness at night (Exodus 13:21). Here in Genesis 8:1, God sends a wind over the earth. Right ingredient, wrong recipe card.

Locusts are in the Bible too, as a plague that hit Egypt (Exodus 10:12-15). Not here, though. After God remembers Noah, He sends a wind, and the waters begin to subside. A boat full of animals does NOT need a swarm.

Not in a single day, friend. The text says "The waters receded steadily from the earth, and after 150 days the waters had gone down." (Genesis 8:3) That's a long, slow goodbye for the flood, more like a dough that takes its sweet time to rise.

You've got it. The text says "The waters receded steadily from the earth, and after 150 days the waters had gone down." (Genesis 8:3) Steady is the word. It was a long, slow process, and nobody could rush it.
Ararat it is. "On the seventeenth day of the seventh month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat." (Genesis 8:4) After all that floating, the ark finally has something solid under it.

Gilboa is a real mountain range in the Bible, but it comes up much later, where Saul, Israel's first king, died in battle (1 Samuel 31:1-6). The ark doesn't land there. Genesis 8:4 says it came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.

Samaria comes much later in the Bible. Omri, a king of Israel, bought the hill of Samaria and built a city there (1 Kings 16:24). The ark never makes it anywhere near it. Genesis 8:4 says it came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.

Mountains! "On the first day of the tenth month the tops of the mountains became visible." (Genesis 8:5) After months of nothing but water, the first land to peek out is the highest land. I think Noah was glad to see anything that wasn't wet.
Close, but not yet. Genesis 8:5 says the tops of the mountains became visible. Trees come into the picture later, when the dove brings back a leaf (Genesis 8:11).
No towers yet, friend. A famous tower comes later in Genesis, in the story of Babel (Genesis 11:4). In Genesis 8:5, what becomes visible is the tops of the mountains.
True. Noah sent out a raven, and "It kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth." (Genesis 8:7) That bird kept at it with no days off.

This one's true, friend. Genesis 8:7 says the raven "kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth." The raven stayed out there, going back and forth, the whole time the waters were drying.

explanations.answer: She finds nowhere to land and returns
explanations.explanation: Right on. "The dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him in the ark." (Genesis 8:9) The waters were still covering the surface of all the earth, so there was no place for her to land.

explanations.answer: She stays out until the next morning
explanations.explanation: She doesn't stay out. The text says she returned to Noah in the ark, because the waters were still covering the surface of all the earth (Genesis 8:9). With no place to rest her foot, back she came.

explanations.answer: She builds a nest in a tree
explanations.explanation: No nest on this trip. Genesis 8:9 says she found no place to rest her foot and returned to Noah. With water over the surface of all the earth, there was nowhere to build anything.
An olive leaf, and a fresh one. "The dove returned to him in the evening with a freshly plucked olive leaf in her beak." (Genesis 8:11) That little leaf says something big, and Noah gets the message.

Fig leaves are in the Bible, but they show up much earlier, when Adam and Eve sewed them together for clothes (Genesis 3:7). Here the dove brings back an olive leaf (Genesis 8:11). Wrong tree, friend.
Palm branches come much later, when the crowd waves them as Jesus comes into Jerusalem (John 12:13). The dove isn't carrying one. In Genesis 8:11, it's a freshly plucked olive leaf.

Receded is right. "So Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth." (Genesis 8:11) A freshly plucked leaf tells him something was growing again out there. It's a little leaf with a big message.
It's the opposite, friend. The leaf was freshly plucked, and "Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth." (Genesis 8:11) Receded means the water had gone down, not up.
Stilled isn't the word the text uses. Genesis 8:11 says Noah knew the waters had receded from the earth. That's the news that olive leaf carried.
Not this time. "Noah waited seven more days and sent the dove out again, but this time she did not return to him." (Genesis 8:12) The first two trips, she came back. The third, she didn't.
You've got it. Genesis 8:12 says Noah "sent the dove out again, but this time she did not return to him." Twice she came back, and the third time she stayed out there.
Dry! "Noah removed the covering from the ark and saw that the surface of the ground was dry." (Genesis 8:13) After a whole lot of water, that's a sight.
Not anymore. The text says Noah removed the covering and saw that the surface of the ground was dry (Genesis 8:13). The flooding was over.
No ice in this story, friend. Genesis 8:13 says Noah removed the covering and saw that the surface of the ground was dry. The waters had dried up from the earth.
Leave is right. God says, "Come out of the ark, you and your wife, along with your sons and their wives." (Genesis 8:16) The earth is fully dry, and the door is open.
No repair job. God's words to Noah are "Come out of the ark" (Genesis 8:16). It's time to leave the ark, not fix it.
Sealing the ark would be the opposite of what God says. His words are "Come out of the ark, you and your wife, along with your sons and their wives." (Genesis 8:16) The word is leave.

explanations.answer: So they can spread out and multiply
explanations.explanation: Yes! God says the creatures should come out "so that they can spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it." (Genesis 8:17) The animals have a whole earth waiting for them.

explanations.answer: So Noah can count every one
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a headcount. God's reason is that they can "spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it." (Genesis 8:17) Noah just needs to bring them out.

explanations.answer: So the ark can be taken apart
explanations.explanation: Nothing about taking the ark apart is in the text. God says to bring out the creatures "so that they can spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply upon it." (Genesis 8:17) That's the reason given.

The clean ones. "Taking from every kind of clean animal and clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar." (Genesis 8:20) Noah builds the altar to the LORD first and makes the offering from the clean animals and birds.
The text doesn't sort them into wild and tame. It says Noah took "from every kind of clean animal and clean bird." (Genesis 8:20) Clean is the word that counts here.
Young isn't what the text says. Noah took "from every kind of clean animal and clean bird." (Genesis 8:20) The sorting is by clean, not by age.
True. The LORD says in His heart, "Never again will I curse the ground because of man." (Genesis 8:21) That's a promise worth holding onto.
This one's true, friend. "Never again will I curse the ground because of man," says the LORD in His heart (Genesis 8:21). That's right in the text.

explanations.answer: It is evil from his youth
explanations.explanation: That's what He says. The LORD says, "even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." (Genesis 8:21) It's a heavy line, and God says it right alongside the promise to never again curse the ground.

explanations.answer: It is pure from his youth
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite, and it's a heavy line. The LORD says, "even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." (Genesis 8:21) Right after that, He promises to never again destroy all living creatures.

explanations.answer: It is humble from his youth
explanations.explanation: Humble isn't the word. The LORD says, "even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth." (Genesis 8:21) It's a heavy thing to say, and He says it while making a promise.
It's the other way around, friend. The LORD says in His heart, "And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done." (Genesis 8:21) That's a promise, not a warning.
Right. What the LORD says in His heart is, "And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done." (Genesis 8:21) He promises the opposite of what the card says.
True. God says, "But you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it." (Genesis 9:4) Everything that lives and moves is food for them, with that one rule.
This one is true. After giving them everything that lives and moves as food, God says, "But you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it." (Genesis 9:4) That's the catch.

explanations.answer: God made mankind in His own image
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says, "for in His own image God has made mankind." (Genesis 9:6) That's the reason given for treating human life so seriously.

explanations.answer: Few people are left after the flood
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that reason. God says it's because "in His own image God has made mankind." (Genesis 9:6) The reason is who people are, not how many.

explanations.answer: Men must answer to their rulers
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention rulers here. The reason God gives is "for in His own image God has made mankind." (Genesis 9:6) Human life matters because of whose image it carries.

Not quite. God says His covenant is also "with every living creature that was with you" (Genesis 9:10). The birds, the livestock and every beast that came out of the ark are included, which means the dove too.

Right, it's false. God says He establishes His covenant "with every living creature that was with you—the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth." (Genesis 9:10) Noah's family and the animals are all in it.
Right. God says, "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood." (Genesis 9:11) That's the promise of the covenant.
Famine isn't what God names. His promise is, "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood." (Genesis 9:11) The covenant is about the flood.
The covenant doesn't name fire. God's words are, "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood." (Genesis 9:11) The promise is about waters.
His rainbow! God says, "I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth." (Genesis 9:13) Next time you see one, you know whose it is.
A star isn't the sign here. God says, "I have set My rainbow in the clouds" (Genesis 9:13). The sign of the covenant is a rainbow.
A pillar of cloud is in the Bible, but later, when the LORD goes ahead of Israel by day (Exodus 13:21). It's not the sign here. In Genesis 9:13, God says, "I have set My rainbow in the clouds."
Yes. God says, "I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind." (Genesis 9:15) That's what the rainbow is for.
Gathering isn't mentioned. When the rainbow appears, God says, "I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind." (Genesis 9:15) The word is remember.
Not here. Genesis 9:15 has God saying, "I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of every kind." That's what He does when the rainbow appears.

Everlasting. God says, "I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind that is on the earth." (Genesis 9:16) That word doesn't have an expiration date.

Conditional isn't the word God uses. He says, "I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind that is on the earth." (Genesis 9:16) Everlasting means it keeps going.
Nothing seasonal about it, friend. God calls it "the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of every kind that is on the earth." (Genesis 9:16) This one has no off season.
